answer: First-order proximity only captures the direct, observed links between a pair of vertices (i.e., whether an edge exists between them). Real-world information networks are sparse and noisy, so many genuinely similar nodes never connect directly, and observed edges can be missing or incomplete. Relying on first-order proximity alone therefore fails to capture the broader structural similarity between nodes that share neighborhoods or occupy similar positions (second-order proximity, which compares neighbor distributions, and higher-order proximity, which reflects longer-range connectivity). Embedding methods such as LINE combine first- and second-order proximity to preserve both local and global network structure, because the direct-link signal alone is too sparse and incomplete to represent the full structure of the network.
